subject: chemistry
overview: This unit covers amines and arenediazonium salts: how amines are prepared, their structure and nomenclature, why they are basic and how that basicity changes with structure, the tests that tell primary, secondary and tertiary amines apart, and how diazonium salts convert $-NH_2$ into many other groups on a benzene ring. NEET asks 1-3 questions from it every year, mostly on reagent-product matching, basicity order, distinguishing tests and conversion sequences built on NCERT reactions.

topics.explanation: Amines are prepared mainly by five routes. Nitro compounds are reduced with $Sn/HCl$, $Fe/HCl$ or $H_2/Pd$; $Fe/HCl$ is preferred because the $FeCl_2$ formed is hydrolysed back to $HCl$. Alkyl halides undergo ammonolysis, but this gives a mixture of 1°, 2° and 3° amines and the quaternary salt. Nitriles are reduced with $LiAlH_4$, $H_2/Ni$ or $Na/C_2H_5OH$; amides are reduced with $LiAlH_4$ followed by $H_2O$. Gabriel phthalimide synthesis gives pure 1° aliphatic amines only. Hofmann bromamide degradation gives a 1° amine with one carbon fewer than the amide. Lower amines are gases or liquids with a fishy smell. Their boiling points are lower than those of alcohols because N-H...N hydrogen bonds are weaker than O-H...O bonds. Key reactions are alkylation, acylation, benzoylation, the carbylamine reaction, reaction with $HNO_2$ and electrophilic substitution in aniline. Amines are used in dyes, drugs and polymers.
key_points: Reduction of nitrobenzene with $Sn/HCl$ or $Fe/HCl$ followed by neutralisation gives aniline; $NaBH_4$ does not reduce $-NO_2$ to $-NH_2$
$RCN \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} RCH_2NH_2$: benzonitrile gives benzylamine, not aniline
$RCONH_2 \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4,\ H_2O} RCH_2NH_2$: the carbon count is retained
Hofmann bromamide: $RCONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow RNH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O$, so the amine has one carbon less; benzamide gives aniline
Gabriel synthesis cannot make aromatic 1° amines, because aryl halides do not undergo $S_N$ reaction with the phthalimide anion
Ammonolysis of alkyl halides gives a mixture; using excess $NH_3$ favours the 1° amine
Acid hydrolysis of acetanilide gives aniline, since the amide bond is cleaved
Boiling points follow 1° > 2° > 3° for isomeric amines; 3° amines have no N-H bond and cannot hydrogen bond among themselves
Bromine water converts aniline to a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline
Direct nitration of aniline gives a large amount of meta product (about 47%) because the anilinium ion forms in acid; acetylation first gives mainly the para product
Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions, because the $-NH_2$ group forms a salt with $AlCl_3$ and deactivates the ring
Sulphonation of aniline gives sulphanilic acid, which exists as a zwitterion
Aniline darkens on storage because it is oxidised by air

topics.topic: General methods of preparation, properties, reactions and uses

topics.explanation: Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. They are classified as primary ($RNH_2$), secondary ($R_2NH$) or tertiary ($R_3N$); $R_4N^+X^-$ is a quaternary ammonium salt. In common names, alkylamine is written as one word (methylamine). In IUPAC names, the 'e' of the alkane is replaced by 'amine' (ethanamine). Substituents on nitrogen are shown with the locant N (N-methylethanamine). Aniline, $C_6H_5NH_2$, is accepted as the IUPAC name benzenamine. In aliphatic amines, nitrogen is $sp^3$ hybridised and pyramidal, and the lone pair occupies the fourth orbital. The C-N-C angle in trimethylamine is about $108^\circ$, close to tetrahedral. In aniline, the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, which gives nitrogen partial $sp^2$ character and a flatter geometry.
key_points: Classification depends on the number of carbons attached to nitrogen, not on the carbon bearing $-NH_2$; tert-butylamine is a 1° amine
Examples of IUPAC names: $CH_3NHC_2H_5$ is N-methylethanamine and $(CH_3)_2NC_6H_5$ is N,N-dimethylbenzenamine
Diamines are named with the suffix diamine, for example $H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2$ is hexane-1,6-diamine
Benzylamine ($C_6H_5CH_2NH_2$) is an aliphatic amine (phenylmethanamine), not an aryl amine
Toluidines are methylanilines and anisidines are methoxyanilines
Aliphatic amine nitrogen is $sp^3$ and pyramidal, with bond angles of about $108^\circ$
The general formula of saturated acyclic amines is $C_nH_{2n+3}N$

topics.explanation: Amines are Lewis and Brønsted bases because nitrogen carries a lone pair. Basicity is measured by $K_b$ or $pK_b$: the larger the $K_b$ (or the smaller the $pK_b$), the stronger the base. Alkyl groups raise basicity through their +I effect. In water, however, the order is also controlled by solvation through hydrogen bonding and by steric hindrance. For methyl amines the order in water is $(CH_3)_2NH > CH_3NH_2 > (CH_3)_3N > NH_3$. For ethyl amines it is $(C_2H_5)_2NH > (C_2H_5)_3N > C_2H_5NH_2 > NH_3$. In the gas phase only the inductive effect operates, so the order is 3° > 2° > 1° > $NH_3$. Aryl amines are much weaker bases ($pK_b$ of aniline is 9.38) because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring and the anilinium ion has fewer resonance structures. Electron-donating ring groups raise basicity and electron-withdrawing groups lower it.
key_points: Overall order: aliphatic amines > $NH_3$ > aryl amines
p-Toluidine ($pK_b$ 8.92) and p-anisidine ($pK_b$ 8.70) are more basic than aniline
p-Nitroaniline ($pK_b$ about 13.0) is much less basic than aniline because $-NO_2$ shows -R and -I effects
Benzylamine is more basic than aniline because its lone pair is not delocalised into the ring
N-Methylaniline and N,N-dimethylaniline are slightly more basic than aniline
Amines form salts with mineral acids, for example $C_6H_5NH_3^+Cl^-$; treating the salt with $NaOH$ regenerates the amine
Amides are almost neutral because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl group

topics.explanation: Three tests distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines. In the Hinsberg test, the amine reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride ($C_6H_5SO_2Cl$). A 1° amine gives an N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide, which dissolves in alkali because its N-H is acidic. A 2° amine gives an N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has no acidic H and is insoluble in alkali. A 3° amine does not react. The carbylamine (isocyanide) test is given only by 1° amines, aliphatic or aromatic: heating with $CHCl_3$ and alcoholic $KOH$ produces a foul-smelling isocyanide. Nitrous acid ($NaNO_2 + HCl$) also distinguishes the classes. 1° aliphatic amines liberate $N_2$ gas. 1° aromatic amines give diazonium salts at 273-278 K. 2° amines give yellow oily N-nitrosamines. 3° aliphatic amines form soluble salts, while 3° aromatic amines undergo ring nitrosation at the para position.
key_points: Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride; p-toluenesulphonyl chloride works the same way
1° amine gives a sulphonamide that is soluble in $KOH$; 2° gives one that is insoluble; 3° gives no reaction
The carbylamine test is positive only for 1° amines, both aliphatic and aromatic
1° aliphatic amines with $HNO_2$ give effervescence of $N_2$ and a mixture of products (alcohol, alkene)
Aniline with $NaNO_2/HCl$ at 273-278 K gives benzenediazonium chloride without evolving $N_2$
2° amines with $HNO_2$ give yellow, oily N-nitrosamines, which are carcinogenic
N,N-Dimethylaniline with $HNO_2$ gives p-nitroso-N,N-dimethylaniline, a green solid

formulas.meaning: Carbylamine test, positive only for 1° amines

Hinsberg reaction; the product dissolves in alkali

topics.neet_tip: Typical questions ask which test distinguishes a given pair of amines, or which statement about Hinsberg or carbylamine behaviour is correct.

topics.explanation: Arenediazonium salts, $ArN_2^+X^-$, are made by diazotisation: a 1° aromatic amine is treated with $NaNO_2 + HCl$ at 273-278 K. They are stable only in cold solution, and arene salts are more stable than alkyl ones because of resonance with the ring. Because $N_2$ is an excellent leaving group, the $-N_2^+$ group can be replaced by Cl, Br or CN (Sandmeyer reaction with Cu(I) salts, or Gattermann reaction with Cu/HX), by I (with $KI$), by F (heating the fluoroborate), by H (with $H_3PO_2$ or ethanol), by OH (warm water) or by $NO_2$. This makes them the standard route to fluoro- and iodobenzenes and to substitution patterns that direct substitution cannot give, such as 1,3,5-tribromobenzene. In coupling reactions the $N_2$ group is retained: with phenol in alkaline medium they give orange p-hydroxyazobenzene, and with aniline in mildly acidic medium they give yellow p-aminoazobenzene. These coloured azo compounds are used as dyes.
key_points: Diazotisation is carried out at 273-278 K because the salt decomposes to phenol and $N_2$ at higher temperatures
Sandmeyer reactions: $CuCl/HCl$ gives $ArCl$, $CuBr/HBr$ gives $ArBr$, $CuCN/KCN$ gives $ArCN$
Gattermann reaction: copper powder with $HCl$ or $HBr$ gives $ArCl$ or $ArBr$
Iodobenzene forms directly with $KI$ and no catalyst is needed
Fluorobenzene is made by heating $ArN_2^+BF_4^-$ (Balz-Schiemann reaction)
$H_3PO_2$ or $CH_3CH_2OH$ replaces $-N_2^+$ by H; this is used to remove $-NH_2$ after it has served as a directing group
Warming in water gives phenol, $ArOH$
$ArN_2^+BF_4^-$ with $NaNO_2/Cu$ on heating gives nitrobenzene
Coupling is electrophilic substitution, usually at the para position, and the $N_2$ group is retained
The sequence aniline, then $Br_2$ water, then diazotisation, then $H_3PO_2$ gives 1,3,5-tribromobenzene

Coupling with phenol gives an orange azo dye

common_traps: Assuming benzonitrile with $LiAlH_4$ gives aniline. It gives benzylamine, $C_6H_5CH_2NH_2$, because the cyano carbon is kept.
Thinking $NaBH_4$ reduces nitrobenzene to aniline. $NaBH_4$ is a mild hydride reagent that does not reduce $-NO_2$; use $Sn/HCl$, $Fe/HCl$ or $H_2/Pd$.
Assuming 3° amines are the most basic in water. Solvation and steric effects make 2° amines the strongest; 3° amines are strongest only in the gas phase.
Using Gabriel synthesis to make aniline. It fails because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.
Expecting only o/p products from direct nitration of aniline. Protonation gives the meta-directing $-NH_3^+$ group, so about 47% of the product is meta; protect the group by acetylation first.
Classifying tert-butylamine as a 3° amine. It is 1° because nitrogen is bonded to only one carbon.
Thinking 2° or 3° amines give the carbylamine test. Only 1° amines (aliphatic and aromatic) give an isocyanide.

Assuming electron-withdrawing groups make both acids and amines weaker. A p-$NO_2$ group strengthens benzoic acid but weakens aniline as a base, while p-$CH_3$ makes p-toluidine more basic than aniline.
quick_revision: Hofmann bromamide removes one carbon; nitrile reduction adds one carbon (as $CH_2$); amide reduction keeps the carbon count.
Gabriel synthesis gives pure 1° aliphatic amines only, never aryl amines.
Boiling points: 1° > 2° > 3° amines, and all are lower than the corresponding alcohols.
Aqueous basicity: $(C_2H_5)_2NH > (C_2H_5)_3N > C_2H_5NH_2 > NH_3$ and $(CH_3)_2NH > CH_3NH_2 > (CH_3)_3N > NH_3$.
Aryl amines are weaker bases than $NH_3$; the $pK_b$ of aniline is 9.38.
Electron-donating groups ($-CH_3$, $-OCH_3$) raise the basicity of aniline; electron-withdrawing groups ($-NO_2$, $-Cl$) lower it.
Hinsberg test: 1° sulphonamide is alkali-soluble, 2° is insoluble, 3° does not react.
Carbylamine test (foul-smelling isocyanide) is given only by 1° amines.
With $HNO_2$: 1° aliphatic gives $N_2$, 1° aromatic gives a diazonium salt, 2° gives a yellow N-nitrosamine.
Aniline gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline with bromine water, gives sulphanilic acid on sulphonation and does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions.
Diazonium reagents: Sandmeyer uses Cu(I) salts, Gattermann uses Cu/HX, $KI$ gives $ArI$, $HBF_4$ then heat gives $ArF$, $H_3PO_2$ gives $ArH$, warm water gives $ArOH$.
Coupling: phenol in alkaline medium gives an orange azo dye; aniline in mildly acidic medium gives a yellow azo dye; substitution is at the para position and $N_2$ is retained.
